caption:
How can a plant with no muscles snap shut in a tenth of a second?

A flytrap's two lobes are held curved outward, under real elastic strain. Water pressure inside the cells slowly bends them toward a tipping point. Touch a trigger hair twice within about twenty seconds and the trap is armed. The second touch sends an electrical signal that tells those cells to dump their water.

Cells on one side release their pressure, and the curved shape turns unstable. Past a certain curve the lobe can no longer hold its bowed shape, and the strain flips it inside out. So the plant never moves quickly. It loads slowly and releases suddenly, and that flip is called snap-buckling.

A slap bracelet flattens the same way, because bending it past a point flips the whole curved strip. And a froghopper's jump uses a stored spring, since muscle alone cannot deliver that power fast enough.

caption:
Why does the grid push power at four hundred thousand volts?

That voltage is dangerous and expensive. There must be a reason. Power is voltage times current, so one big number lets the other shrink. The wires themselves waste power by heating up as charge flows through.

That waste depends on the current squared, not on the voltage. More current means both more charge pushed and a harder push, so the heat rises twice over. Raise the voltage twenty times, and the wasted heat drops four hundred times. Twenty times the voltage means a twentieth of the current, and a twentieth squared is four hundred times less heat. So sending the same power at higher voltage means far less current.

Less current means dramatically less heat left behind in the cables.

So the grid trades current for volts to save power. Heat wasted in the wires is called I squared R loss.

A long extension cord gets warm running a heater, because the same current wastes power in every metre. And your phone charger sends five volts only a short way, since a long low-voltage run would waste most energy.

caption:
Why does one thin wire glow while the thick wires beside it stay dark?

They are joined in one line, so the same current passes through all. Same current, and yet only one of them gets hot enough to shine. A thin wire has less room for the charge to move through.

That makes it resist the flow more in every centimetre of its length. Halve the width and you roughly quadruple the resistance. Heating depends on the current squared, times that resistance. Charges forced through a tight wire keep banging into its atoms, and that jostling is heat.

So with the current fixed, the thinnest piece dumps by far the most heat.

So all the wires carry one current. The thin one simply turns more of it into heat. That is called Joule heating.

A fuse protects your house by being the thinnest link, so it melts before the wiring behind the walls does. And a toaster element glows orange for the same reason. It is made deliberately thin and long to resist the current.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does a magnet fall slowly down a copper pipe that is not magnetic?

Drop a steel bolt through and it clatters straight out. The magnet crawls. Copper is packed with tiny charges called electrons that can drift freely. As the magnet falls, the magnetism through each ring of pipe keeps changing.

A changing magnetism drives those charges around the pipe in circling currents. A bolt drops a metre in half a second. The magnet takes eight. Each circling current is itself a small magnet, and it fights the change. If it helped the fall the magnet would speed up for free, so it must always oppose.

So the pipe above pulls the magnet up, and the pipe below pushes back.

So the copper stays unmagnetised. Its own circling currents resist the falling magnet, and that rule is called Lenz's law.

A train can brake without touching the rail. A magnet sweeping past metal stirs currents that drag it to a stop. An induction hob drives these same circling currents through a steel pan. The pan heats itself, while the glass stays cool.

caption:
Why does heat reach only a sliver of the tiny charges called electrons in a metal?

A metal is a stiff grid of atoms with those charges free to roam. By the old classical rules every one of them should soak up heat. But two of these charges cannot share the same state of motion, so they stack up.

They fill every level from the bottom up to a sharp top edge. Room warmth is a nudge of one fortieth of a volt. That stack is seven volts deep. A charge buried deep has no empty level to enter, so warmth cannot shift it.

Only the ones within a nudge of the top edge have somewhere to go.

So the metal is not being lazy. Only the charges at that top edge can answer. We call it the Fermi surface.

A metal's heat capacity rises straight in step with temperature, because a bigger nudge simply frees a thicker shell. An electric current works the same way, since only charges beside that edge find empty states to move into.

What did you think the reason was?

caption:
Why can a car never slide sideways, yet still park sideways?

Push a parked car from the side and it refuses. The tyres dig in. A rolling wheel can go where it points, forwards or backwards, and nowhere else. So at any instant your car has two choices: roll, and turn the steering.

Sideways is not on that list, at any single instant. But roll forward turning left, then back turning right, and repeat. The two arcs curve opposite ways, so the car comes back beside where it started, not onto it. Each pass shifts you about half a metre toward the kerb.

Four passes and you have moved two metres sideways, using only allowed moves.

So sideways is blocked at every instant, but not over time. A sequence reaches places no single move can. That restriction is called a nonholonomic constraint.

A shopping trolley with fixed rear wheels is shuffled sideways the same way, by wiggling it forwards and back. And a cat in mid air turns around by twisting its body through a loop, using shape changes only.

Which part of this surprised you?

caption:
Why does everything look blurred underwater until you put goggles on?

Your eye is not harmed, and the pool water is perfectly clear. Most of your eye's focusing is not done by the lens inside it. It happens at the front surface, where air meets the wet cornea.

Light bends there because air and the eye's fluid slow light very differently. But water slows light almost exactly as much as your eye does. So with water in front, that surface has almost nothing left to bend.

Two thirds of your focusing power vanishes, and the image lands behind the retina. The retina catches the light before it comes to a point, so every dot lands as a smear.

So goggles change nothing inside the eye. They put air back in front. That bending strength is called refractive power.

A fish eye carries a nearly spherical lens, because its front surface gets no help from the surrounding water. And a contact lens works by reshaping that same front surface, where the strongest bend in your eye happens.

caption:
Why does a 7 tera electron volts proton hitting a wall waste most of its energy?

You might expect all seven trillion volts to go into making new particles. But the target's atoms sit still, while the proton is racing forward. Whatever they make must keep moving forward too, to balance the push.

That forward motion carries energy away, and it cannot be spent on mass. Only the energy seen in the collision's own frame can build anything. Ride along with the wreckage, and whatever energy is left over there is all you can spend. And that shared energy grows only as the square root of the beam energy.

So doubling the beam buys you just forty percent more usable energy.

So the proton carries 7 tera electron volts, yet a fixed wall gives only 115 giga electron volts. Two beams head on give 14 tera electron volts. That is the centre of mass energy.

Two cars crashing head on wreck far more than one car hitting a parked car, for the same reason. And the collider rings two beams against each other instead of a target. Is how it reaches fourteen tera electron volts.

caption:
Why does one gas need two different numbers for its heat capacity?

Heat a kilogram of water and you quote one number. Gases refuse that. Seal the gas in a rigid steel box and warm it. Nothing moves. Every bit of heat goes into making the gas hotter, and nothing else.

Now put the same gas under a sliding piston that holds the pressure steady. Warm it and the gas expands, lifting that piston against the air above. Warming makes the gas push harder, so it must swell until its push matches the air again. So part of the heat is spent as work, not as temperature.

To get the same rise in temperature you must supply more heat.

So a gas carries two heat numbers because it can push. The gap between them is called the gas constant.

The speed of sound in air depends on the ratio of these two numbers. That ratio puts it near 340 metres per second. And a hot air balloon works at steady pressure. The warmed air expands and shoves the surrounding air aside.

Who else was taught this wrong?

caption:
Why does cutting a spring in half make it twice as stiff?

Nothing was added. Half the metal is gone, and yet it fights harder. Think of a spring as a chain of identical coils, one behind another. Pull the two ends, and every single coil feels exactly the same pull. Each coil passes the pull straight to the next, so the same force runs the whole length.

So each coil opens by the same small amount, and those openings add up. Twenty coils give forty millimetres of stretch. Ten coils give twenty. Cut it in half and there are half as many coils to add up.

So the same pull buys half the stretch, which is double the stiffness.

So a short spring is not made of stronger metal. It has fewer coils sharing the stretch. That stiffness is called the spring constant.

Fold a rubber band in two and it pulls back far harder. Each half is shorter, and now two share the load. A long steel cable sags far more than a short one. Extra length means more metal sharing the same pull.

caption:
How can a loop of wire add a fifty hertz hum you never measured?

Your instrument reads a clean signal, plus a steady buzz at mains speed. Mains cables in the wall carry current that reverses fifty times a second. A reversing current wraps a magnetic field around itself, growing and collapsing.

Any closed loop of wire sitting in that field feels a push on its charges. Your signal wire and its return travel apart and back, and the space between them is the loop. The bigger the area your cables enclose, the bigger that unwanted push. Half a square metre picks up about three hundred microvolts of hum.

Twist the pair together and the enclosed area nearly vanishes, so the hum collapses.

So nothing you measured made that buzz. Your own cable loop is a pickup coil. That effect is called electromagnetic induction.

An induction hob heats a pan the same way, driving swirling currents in the metal with a changing field. And a metal detector finds coins by the same push, sensing currents its changing field stirs underground.

caption:
Why is one point of a rolling wheel always standing still?

The wheel is racing down the road. Nothing about it looks still. A rolling wheel does two things at once. It moves along and it turns. As long as the tyre does not skid, its rim turns at exactly the speed the car travels. Turning carries the top of the tyre forward, on top of the car's speed.

At sixty, the top of the tyre is doing a hundred and twenty. At the bottom, turning carries the rubber backward just as fast as the car goes forward. Those two motions cancel exactly, so that patch of rubber is briefly at rest.

That is why a tyre grips the road instead of smearing along it.

So a rolling wheel pivots about the patch touching the road. That still point is called the instantaneous axis of rotation.

Photograph a moving bicycle and the top spokes blur away. The rubber near the road is barely moving, so it stays sharp. A tank track lies still where it meets the ground. The top run races forward at twice the tank's speed.

caption:
What actually pushes a car forward when it speeds up?

Not the engine. The engine only presses parts of the car against each other. A push from inside a system cannot shift the whole system. Every push inside comes with an equal push back, so the pair cancels out. So something outside must shove it, and only the road is touching.

The tyres can give about eight thousand newtons. Hard acceleration needs less. The engine turns the wheels, and the tyre presses backward on the tarmac. The tarmac presses forward on the tyre with exactly the same strength.

That forward press from the road is the one force speeding the car up.

So the engine never pushes the car forward. It only lets the road push it, and we call that grip static friction.

A swimmer pushes water backward, and the water pushes her forward, since nothing inside her body could do it. A rocket has no surface to press on, so it throws its own exhaust backward and gets pushed forward.

caption:
Why does almost every system in physics behave like a spring?

A pendulum, a bond between two atoms, and a bridge share one equation. Anything stable sits at the bottom of some energy valley. At the very bottom the slope is zero, or it would roll away. The steeper the valley under your feet, the harder it pushes you back to the bottom.

caption:
Why does the top of a rolling wheel move twice as fast as its axle?

It is one rigid object, so you expect every part to share one speed. But the bottom of a rolling wheel is momentarily standing still. It grips the road without sliding, so the contact point has zero speed.

So the axle moves at the car's speed and the wheel top doubles it. That pivot is called the instantaneous centre.

caption:
How can pumping at exactly twice the rhythm make a swing grow fastest?

Push a swing once each pass and it builds. That is the obvious way. But a child on a swing pushes nothing. There is nobody there. She crouches and stands, changing how far her weight sits from the pivot.

caption:
Why can fifty trapped atoms need a quadrillion numbers to describe them?

Each atom sits in a trap made of light, and can point up or down. Two atoms give four combinations. Three give eight. Each atom doubles the count. Fifty atoms give two multiplied by itself fifty times.

caption:
How does a pool player stop the cue ball dead on impact?

It strikes, stops instantly, and the other ball leaves with all the speed. The trick only works because both balls weigh exactly the same. So the pool player does not stop the cue ball by skill alone. It hands over everything because the weights match. That is an elastic collision.

caption:
Why does a clock on a shelf run faster than one on the floor?

The two clocks are identical. Nothing mechanical is different between them. Gravity does more than pull on things. It also stretches time itself. caption:
Why can very pure water stay liquid at minus forty degrees?

Freezing does not begin everywhere at once. It has to start somewhere. That start is a tiny speck of ice, perhaps a hundred atoms across. Building it releases energy inside, but it costs energy at the surface.

caption:
Why does a magnet grip your fridge but slide straight off a soda can?

Both are metal. Both conduct electricity. Yet only one holds. Every electron inside a metal behaves like a tiny magnet, with its own north and south. In most materials those tiny magnets point every which way and cancel out.

caption:
How can a longer ramp get a ball down faster than a straight one?

Take two points, one metre across and one metre down, and roll a bead. The straight ramp is the shortest path, so it should surely be quickest. But speed comes from how far you have already dropped, not how far you travelled. Every metre you fall is turned into speed, no matter which way you came down.

The curved ramp dives steeply at the start, so the bead gains speed early. It travels further, yet it spends most of that distance moving fast. Dropping late is expensive, because you crawl through the whole first stretch.

The winning shape is the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel.

So the straight ramp wins on length and loses on time. The longer curve is faster. That shape is called the brachistochrone.

A skateboarder drops into a curved ramp rather than a flat slope, gaining speed early for the same reason. And light crossing into glass takes the quickest path rather than the shortest, which is the very same trade.

caption:
Why does adding more waves never flatten the ripple at a sharp jump?

A square wave can be built by adding smooth waves of rising pitch. Add ten of them and the shape is close, but the corners ring. Add a thousand and the ringing looks thinner, so you expect it to fade.

It does not. The first spike stays about nine percent above the jump. Each extra wave makes the ripple narrower, but it also makes it steeper. Smooth waves cannot turn a corner instantly, so the sum always swings past before settling. The width shrinks while the height holds, so the spike just crowds the corner.

Averaged over any small window the error does vanish, so the fit really improves.

So the ripple never shrinks in height. It only shrinks in width. That stubborn overshoot is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

A sharp edge in a compressed photo shows the same ringing halo, because the picture is built from waves. And an audio filter with a hard cutoff rings the same way, adding a faint click before the sound.

caption:
Why can a lone neutron decay when one inside deuterium cannot?

A free neutron lasts about fifteen minutes, then turns into a proton. It can do that because a proton weighs slightly less than a neutron. That leftover mass becomes energy, about zero point seven eight mega electron volts.

Why is a thermometer still thirty-seven percent wrong after one response time?

caption:
Why does a camera invent a spin that was never really there?

A film is not motion. It is only a row of still snapshots. Between two snapshots the wheel keeps turning, and the camera sees none of it. If a spoke turns almost a full gap between frames, it lands just short. Every spoke looks the same, so you cannot tell one spoke from the next one.

Why is calm air made of particles racing at five hundred metres per second?

That is faster than a rifle bullet, in a room where nothing stirs. Air is made of tiny particles called molecules, flying in all directions. Temperature is just a measure of how fast they are typically moving.

At room temperature the average speed really is about five hundred metres per second. Huge individual speeds. An average of almost exactly zero. Each one picks its direction at random, and there are countless of them.

For every particle heading left, another heads right just as fast, so the crowd goes nowhere.

So the particles are wildly fast and the air still stays calm. Wind is only the leftover drift, and the rest is called random thermal motion.

A smell crosses a room in minutes, not milliseconds, because each molecule zigzags through billions of collisions on the way. And the pressure holding a balloon open is those particles drumming on the rubber, billions of times a second.

Why does covering half a lens dim the picture instead of cutting it in half?

Half the glass is blocked. You expect half the scene to vanish. But every part of a lens sees the whole scene. Light from one scene point spreads across the entire lens.

The glass bends all of those rays back to one spot on the sensor. A full lens gathers every ray. Half the lens gathers half of them. So blocking half the glass removes half the rays heading to every point.

Every point of the picture survives, just carrying half the light.

So a lens does not carve the picture into pieces. Each patch of glass builds a full picture, and the opening that sets brightness is called the aperture.

A dust spot on a telescope mirror hides no star. It only removes a small share of the light from every point. Squinting narrows the pupil and darkens the view, yet you still see the whole room, only dimmer and sharper.

Who else was taught this wrong?
